Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is my honor to brief you on the 25th Session of the Committee of Experts on Public Administration held from 13 to 17 April 2026 at United Nations Headquarters. We met at a moment of profound economic, social, and environmental strain. Progress towards the goals remains severely off track. Challenges extend beyond financing and and include in particular implementation, institutional capacity, and public trust. The 2026 HLPF Ministerial Declaration adopted last week recognizes good governance and strong institutions as key enablers of sustainable development. That recognition goes to the heart of the Committee's deliberations on transformative equitable, innovative, and urgent actions required to rebuild trust, revitalize institutions, and realize the SDGs. Such reforms should include reviewing multi-level governance arrangements to empower all levels of government while encouraging meaningful stakeholder participation, especially at the local level. These efforts must be grounded in evidence. Our work on the principles of effective governance and the committee's pentagram of action provides a practical compass. Our findings confirm that the quality of governance remains critical to progress across the goals. Action-oriented diagnostic tools can identify institutional constraints, close implementation gaps, and sequence reforms around high-impact priorities. In support of the Sevilla Commitment, we identified urgent priorities for resource mobilization and public financial management. These include more resilient fiscal frameworks, stronger subnational financial management, better allocation and management of the development finance, and enhanced legal and operational independence of supreme audit institutions. Looking ahead, we outlined 3 pathways towards a future-oriented public administration: 1, anticipatory governance; 2, evidence-informed administration; 3, agile and adaptive administration. We also examined artificial intelligence as both a transformative opportunity and a profound governance challenge. Its use should expand public value and administrative capability underpinned by clear governance arrangements for procurement, human oversight, auditability, inclusion, respect for human rights, and protection against bias. Yet institutions must ultimately be judged by whom they serve and whom they include. Trust grows when people feel heard and protected. This imperative shaped our considerations of use unemployment. We called for general, integrated, gender-sensitive youth employment frameworks linking education and labor ministries, local authorities, and the private sector to promote decent jobs, technological skills, and entrepreneurship. The same institutional lens shaped our work on water, where we stressed that water security depends on strong institutions supported by governance diagnostics to identify constraints and sequence reforms at the national level. Finally, 6 voluntary national review countries joined a peer exchange on the institutional aspects of Goal 16 and 17, turning experience into shared learning and better practice. Mr. Vice President, our message is clear: accelerating progress towards the SDGs requires public administration transformation. This means moving from reactive policymaking to strengthening capable, accountable, and inclusive institutions. Trust is built when those institutions demonstrate they can listen, learn, and deliver for everyone today and for generations to come. I thank you.

Distinguished representatives, ladies and gentlemen, greetings from Vienna. It is my pleasure to brief the Council on the outcomes of the 35th Session of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice and to provide an update on preparations for the 15th United Nations Crime Congress. The 35th session, held in Vienna from the 1st to the 5th of June 2026, reaffirmed the Commission's continued relevance and attracted broad participation. We welcomed around 1,500 participants representing 126 member states, in addition to representatives from United Nations entities, intergovernmental organizations, and civil society. The 3 resolutions adopted by the Commission at its 35th session address several important emerging issues. First, Member States adopted a resolution aimed at strengthening crime prevention and criminal justice responses to prevent and combat fraud, to be recommended by the Economic and Social Council for adoption by the General Assembly. The Commission also adopted 2 resolutions to be brought to the attention of the Council, one addressing the prevention and combating of transnational sexual extortion of children, commonly referred to as sextortion, and another focusing on countering trafficking in persons for the purpose of forced criminality. Allow me now to turn to preparations for the 15th United Nations Crime Congress, for which the CCP CJ acts as preparatory and main follow-up body. Following its postponement in April, the Congress will be held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, from the 26th of September to the 1st of October 2026, with pre-session consultations taking place on the 25th of September. The Congress, as the largest UN gathering on crime prevention and criminal justice matters, happening every 5 years, provides a unique platform to advance global action, bringing together governments, international organizations, civil society, and individual experts. The agenda of the Congress has been designed to address both current and emerging challenges from innovative crime prevention people-centered justice systems, new and evolving forms of crime, to strengthening international cooperation and technical assistance. Complementing these agenda items are 4 workshops focusing on resilient societies, equal access to justice, better use of data and evidence, and the responsible use of technology in crime prevention and criminal justice. Let me now turn to one of the key highlights of the Congress. The High-Level Segment will bring together heads of state and government, ministers, and other senior representatives to reaffirm the international community's commitment to strengthening crime prevention, criminal justice, and the rule of law. In addition, the High-Level Segment will feature a series of thematic meetings that will promote dialogue on key priorities. A central milestone of the Congress will be the adoption of the Abu Dhabi Declaration, which will provide strategic guidance for international cooperation in the years ahead. I would also like to encourage all delegations to participate actively in the Pledge for Justice initiative, which offers an opportunity to showcase concrete national and international commitments supporting implementation of the Congress outcomes. An important strength of the Crime Congress is its ability to bring together a truly diverse range of stakeholders. Youth engagement is a central component. A youth forum will be held on the 24th till the 25th of September, prepared by the GenJust, the Generation Justice initiative. The Congress will also introduce fireside chats with the private sector, providing an opportunity to exchange views on innovation, technology, and partnerships in addressing evolving crime challenges. Participants will also benefit from a rich program of over 200 ancillary events and some 40 exhibitions. Finally, I would like to highlight the written contribution which I submitted in my chair's capacity to the 2026 High-Level Political Forum. It highlights action taken by the CCBCJ on crimes affecting the environment, trafficking in persons, crime prevention, and prison management, among other areas. I thank you very much, and I wish you fruitful discussions.

Distinguished delegates, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to present the report on the 25th Session of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, held from 20 April to 1 May 2026 at United Nations Headquarters. The report, as contained in Document E/2026/43, reflects discussions and recommendations that emerged from dialogue among Indigenous Peoples, Member States, and other stakeholders on some of the most pressing issues facing Indigenous Peoples today. I would like to thank Indigenous Peoples, Member States, UN entities, and all other participants whose engagement enriched the Forum's deliberations and contributed to a successful session. The special theme of the 25th session was Ensuring Indigenous Peoples' Health, including in the context of conflict. Throughout the session, a clear message emerged: Indigenous Peoples' health cannot be separated from their lands, territories, cultures, languages, and right to self-determination. The Forum emphasized that the implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples remains fundamental to advancing the health, well-being, and the rights of Indigenous Peoples. Free, prior, and informed consent remains a cornerstone of that effort. The Forum also examined the growing impacts of climate change on Indigenous peoples across all regions. Indigenous peoples continue to experience severe impacts on their lands, livelihoods, food systems, cultures, and health, despite, despite contributing the least to global greenhouse gas emissions. The Forum called for climate action and energy transition policies to fully respect Indigenous Peoples' rights and to ensure their effective participation in climate governance and decision-making processes. At the same time, the Forum expressed concern regarding the increasing pressures associated with extractive activities and the growing demand for critical minerals. The Forum stressed that climate action and development initiatives must not come at the expense of Indigenous Peoples' rights, lands, and territories, and that free, prior, and informed consent must be fully respected. Particular attention was also given to the impacts of conflict, displacement, and environmental degradation on Indigenous peoples' communities, especially Indigenous women and girls. The Forum expressed concern over continuing human rights violations, including gender-based violence, forced sterilization, and barriers to health services and participation, and called for stronger protections and accountability measures. Across all areas of work, the Forum emphasized the importance of meaningful participation. Indigenous Peoples must be recognized as rights holders and decision makers in processes that affect their lives. In this regard, the Forum has proposed an international expert group meeting on the theme of enhanced participation of Indigenous Peoples. The Forum also considered ongoing United Nations reform efforts, including UNAD Initiative. It underscored that these reforms should strengthen rather than diminish the meaningful participation of Indigenous Peoples and the distinct roles of the UN mechanisms dedicated to Indigenous Peoples. Distinguished delegates, The report before you contains recommendations for Member States, United Nations entities, and other stakeholders that advance human rights, sustainable development, peace, and environmental stewardship, including through the effective implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. In doing so, the Forum contributes directly to advancing Sustainable Development Objectives including support to the principle of leaving no one behind. The Forum's recommendations strengthen the work of ECOSOC by bringing Indigenous Peoples' perspectives and knowledge systems into discussions on sustainable development, climate action, health, financing, and governance. The Forum has proposed that its 26th session be held from 10 21st, May 2027, at United Nations Headquarters. The session will take place at a particularly significant moment as the international community marks the 20th anniversary of the Declaration. Recognizing the continued importance of strengthening Indigenous Peoples' voices within the United Nations processes, the Forum will continue to focus on advancing implementation of the Declaration and promoting the full and effective participation of Indigenous Peoples in decision-making at all levels. The Forum remains committed to its continued engagement with ECOSOC and the wider United Nations system to ensure that Indigenous Peoples' knowledge, perspectives, priorities, and solutions continue to inform global policymaking and advance sustainable, cohesive, and resilient societies. I thank you for your attention, and I remain at your disposal for any questions you may have. Hoi an nameng. Thank you.

Mr. President, for the Russian Federation, issues having to do with the situation of indigenous peoples are of particular significance. Their basic rights have been enshrined in our Constitution and the legislation of our country. To ensure they are effectively upheld on a constant basis, there is work being done constantly to improve and renew our national legal and regulatory basis. We've improved our law enforcement practice. We've strengthened prosecutorial oversight for the implementation of laws. In this regard, we are disturbed to see a dismaying trend toward politicization of the work of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Peoples. This is one of the main UN platforms for open, constructive, and mutually respectful dialogue between representatives of governments and Indigenous Peoples. The latest manifestation of something that's been gathering steam, namely the deleterious practice of using human rights issues for geopolitical purposes, is what we've seen, and we roundly reject such an approach. The same goes for the encroachment of the Permanent Forum on the remit of other UN system bodies, in particular on issues relating to the maintenance of International peace and security, for which the Security Council is responsible. I'm referring to paragraphs 52 and 60. There's something that undermines trust in the Permanent Forum and the methods of its work. I'm referring to the use of unverified information. That's in paragraph 53. Information coming from self-proclaimed protectors of Indigenous Peoples, and their destructive activity is carried out outside of Russia, and that activity has nothing in common whatever with genuine human rights work. We recall that Russia, like any other state, has an obligation to stop terrorist and extremist activity seeking to undermine interethnic peace and amity, and to stop activity which poses a threat to the sovereignty of our country. We note that the Permanent Forum has departed from the practice of engaging in a serious analysis of the situation on the ground. In this regard, we would propose to— that the distinguished members of ECOSOC read the report from Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on the situation of indigenous peoples in certain countries. That report is posted on the website of our Foreign Ministry. Mr. President, the use with regard to Russia in paragraph 11 of language such as displacement of populations, the loss of livelihoods, or the erosion of knowledge stems from an ignorance of the situation in Russia. Either that or it's a deliberate distortion. We have our own unique experience in upholding the rights of small-numbered indigenous peoples. This allows us in this day and age to maintain their numbers, language, traditional forms of life. We've set up mechanisms for indigenous small-numbered peoples to participate in decision-making, to participate in environmental expert reports and in public hearings. During the planning and implementation of economic activities and industrial projects that are carried out on their traditional lands. Models of partnership of Russian business and small number of indigenous peoples are— is carried out only within the Russian legal framework. When disputes arrive— when disputes arise, they can be resolved in the courts or through arbitration. The development of recommendations based on incomplete or distorted information, coupled with the brazen bias of certain experts of the Permanent Forum who don't want to establish and support dialogue with states, is undermining the efficiency of the mandate of the Permanent Forum and the trust in it. Given the foregoing, we— our delegation disassociates itself from the consensus on the decision taking note of the report of the 25th session of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and we ask you to reflect this in the record of the meeting. Thank you.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, with fewer than 4 years remaining until 2030, The defining challenge is no longer agreeing on ambition, but rather accelerating implementation. Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The United States disassociates from consensus on the reelection of Cuba to the Commission on Science and Technology for Development. We did not stay in the way of this election, and we did not call a vote. But we cannot let this moment pass without registering our serious concerns, both about Cuba's fitness to serve on this Commission and about the Commission itself. Fundamentally, Cuba is not a serious partner on the issues within this Commission's mandate. The Cuban government suppresses the free flow of information, controls internet access, and restricts its own citizens' ability to innovate, communicate, and engage with the digital economy. A regime that polices its own people's access to information and technology has no credible claim to help shape global science, technology, and innovation policy. We do not believe Cuba's record reflects the values we hope this commission would represent, and we do not believe its membership will advance the commission's stated purpose. Our concerns about this election are compounded by our concerns about the commission itself. As the United States has stated As stated in prior sessions, the resolutions that emerge from this Commission have become bloated, unfocused, and increasingly disconnected from the practical work of advancing technology for development. Rather than a serious forum for science and technology cooperation, we have too often seen this body used to relitigate broader ideological debates that belong elsewhere. These are not new concerns. Concerns. They are the same concerns that led the United States to vote against this Commission's core resolution in 2025, and they are why the United States did not seek reelection to this Commission for the next term. Our decision not to run reflects our judgment that this body, as currently constituted, is not delivering results proportionate to the resources member states devote to it.
